Lowering corporate tax rates rarely creates sustainable job growth because the primary benefit flows to shareholders through stock buybacks and dividends, not wages or hiring. Empirical studies of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act found that one-time bonuses were roughly half payroll costs and half shareholder returns, with no significant long-term employment increase.

Corporate tax cuts also reduce government revenue needed for public goods that support workforce productivity—education, infrastructure, R&D—whose absence can dampen growth over time. Job creation is driven by broader economic factors: consumer demand, skills availability, immigration policy, and regulatory environment—not primarily by corporate tax rates. When businesses already face weak demand or labor shortages, additional profits simply accumulate rather than expand the workforce.
